item.title: IMF projects 7 pc growth for India, Piyush Goyal hails forecast

item.content:encoded:
IMF projects 7 pc growth for India, Piyush Goyal hails forecast The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday projected India's economy to grow by 7 per cent in both FY27 and FY28, while warning of a fragile global economic outlook, rising inflation, geopolitical uncertainties and mounting fiscal pressures across major economies. ANI | Updated: 13-10-2026 23:05 IST | Created: 13-10-2026 23:05 IST

Representative image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday projected India's economy to grow by 7 per cent in both FY27 and FY28, while warning of a fragile global economic outlook, rising inflation, geopolitical uncertainties and mounting fiscal pressures across major economies. The projection, released in the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook, was welcomed by Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, who said India's free trade agreements (FTAs) would further strengthen global economic activity and resilient supply chains. The IMF projected global growth to slow from 3.5 per cent in 2025 to 3.1 per cent in 2026 before recovering to 3.4 per cent in 2027. “The global economy remains resilient, but that resilience is becoming more fragile and more uneven,” the Fund said. India, however, is expected to remain among the fastest-growing major economies, supported by stronger-than-expected economic momentum, resilient domestic demand and robust services activity. Reacting to the forecast, Goyal said in a post on X, “UNSTOPPABLE INDIA! IMF has projected a 7% GDP growth for 2027 for Bharat, making us among the fastest growing major economies. Our multiple FTAs under PM @NarendraModi ji are also expected to positively contribute to global economic activity and build resilient supply chains.” On global inflation, the IMF projected an increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026, driven by higher energy and food prices, before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027. It warned that prolonged conflict or further escalation in the Middle East could keep commodity prices elevated, revive inflationary pressures and weaken economic growth. “Risks are skewed to the downside,” the report said. The IMF also cautioned that global trade growth could slow amid tariffs, supply-chain adjustments and geopolitical disruptions, despite support from technology-related investment and trade. It flagged the possibility of a sharp reassessment of artificial intelligence-related investment returns, which could trigger equity market corrections and tighten financial conditions. Separately, the Fund raised concerns over deteriorating fiscal conditions, noting that public debt remained elevated and fiscal deficits in several major economies were significantly higher than before the COVID-19 pandemic. Rising borrowing costs, alongside spending pressures related to ageing populations, climate change and national security, have further reduced governments' ability to respond to fresh economic shocks. The IMF called for “strong and deliberate actions” to rebuild fiscal buffers and strengthen resilience, warning that the room for policy adjustments was narrowing. While India's growth outlook remains relatively strong, the Fund's broader assessment highlighted increasing vulnerabilities in the global economy from persistent geopolitical tensions, inflationary pressures and limited fiscal space. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis also hailed the forecast made by IMF. "India Defies the Odds! The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects India’s economy to grow by 7.0% in both 2026 and 2027, making us among the fastest growing major economies. Under the visionary leadership of Hon PM Narendra Modi Ji, India continues to emerge as a driving force of global growth despite ongoing global economic uncertainties," he wrote on X. Union Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat also hailed the projections. "Under the visionary leadership of Hon’ble PM Shri @narendramodi ji, India continues to demonstrate remarkable economic resilience and strong growth momentum amid global uncertainty. The IMF projects India’s GDP to grow at 7.0% in both 2026 and 2027, even as global growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026 amid rising inflationary pressures. This reflects India’s growing economic strength and its expanding role in the global economy. India continues to advance towards a Viksit Bharat, driven by reforms, investment and sustained economic growth under Hon’ble PM Modi ji’s leadership," he said. Keralam BJP president Rajeev Chandrasekhar said the projections are a result of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's "incredibly deft management of the economy". "India's economy has never been stronger and more resilient. Today the IMF has upgraded India's growth forecast to 7% for 2026-27, far outpacing the fragile global average of 3.1% This is no accident. It is the direct result of PM @narendramodi ji's incredibly deft management of the economy during the pandemic, the biggest challenge of his 25 years in governance. We rightly thank him for how he managed the Covid health crisis. Not many understand how incredibly well he also handled the economic challenge, steering India through the storm and to calmer seas. Since Covid, almost every major economy has seen its public finances worsen," he said. Slamming the opposition, Chandrasekhar added, "India is one of the few whose finances and economic activity are back near pre-Covid levels. No other major economy, not the USA, not China, not Europe, is where India is While the opposition stays fully invested in creating chaos and anarchy at home, the Modi government continues to build a stronger, more resilient India. Meanwhile, spare a thought (or not) for the political frauds who called India's economy dead. These types of results are beyond the comprehension of lazy, clueless, inept, entitled, dynastic leaders and their cronies." (ANI)

Tibetan groups in Europe unite to challenge China’s assimilation drive Organised by the Office of Tibet, London, with support from the Norwegian Tibet Committee and the Tibetan Community in Norway, the gathering followed previous meetings in Sweden in 2023 and Denmark in 2025. Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Analyzing article...

Oslo [Norway], October 13 (ANI) Tibetan civil society organisations from across Europe have joined forces to oppose China’s ethnic unity legislation, raising concerns over its potential impact on Tibetan language, cultural identity and religious heritage. The Third Regional Meeting of Tibetan Civil Society Organisations called for coordinated international advocacy to counter Beijing’s policies, as reported by the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA). According to CTA, the meeting took place at the Karma Shedrubling Retreat Centre, bringing together 25 representatives from seven Tibet Support Groups across Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Lithuania and the United Kingdom. Tibetan community representatives, national coordinators and Tibetan parliamentarian Thupten Gyatso also participated. Organised by the Office of Tibet, London, with support from the Norwegian Tibet Committee and the Tibetan Community in Norway, the gathering followed previous meetings in Sweden in 2023 and Denmark in 2025. Discussions focused on China’s so-called Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress Law, which participants said could further undermine Tibetan identity and promote assimilation. Norwegian historian and journalist Torbjørn Færøvik outlined the legislation’s emphasis on national unity, territorial integrity and political loyalty to the Chinese Communist Party. Participants proposed a series of joint initiatives, including coordinated lobbying campaigns, parliamentary delegations to Dharamshala, information leaflets explaining the law’s implications and stronger cooperation among Nordic countries. Regular engagement with lawmakers and policymakers was also identified as a priority. Gyatso criticised the legislation, describing it as a means of concealing what he called a genocidal programme. He urged Tibetans in exile to protect their heritage and encouraged international supporters to establish Tibetan language and cultural centres in their respective countries, as highlighted by CTA. A separate session on October 11 addressed concerns within Tibetan communities, particularly the declining use of the Tibetan language among younger generations. Community leaders were encouraged to promote mother-tongue education and strengthen cultural ties between parents and children, as reported by CTA. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
Canadian FM Anita Anand on India visit; to hold talks with EAM Jaishankar on trade, energy, security, defence ties Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand is in India as part of her two-nation visit, which also includes the United Arab Emirates from October 13 to October 16, with discussions with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar set to focus on advancing bilateral cooperation in trade, energy, people-to-people ties, and security and defence, amid ongoing negotiations for a comprehensive trade agreement between the two countries. ANI | Updated: 13-10-2026 09:10 IST | Created: 13-10-2026 09:10 IST

External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand (File Photo/X@DrSJaishankar). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand is on an India visit as part of her two-nation tour, which also includes the United Arab Emirates from October 13 to October 16, with discussions with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar set to focus on advancing bilateral cooperation in trade, energy, people-to-people ties, and security and defence, amid ongoing negotiations for a comprehensive trade agreement between the two countries. According to a news release issued by the Canadian government on Monday, Anand will meet EAM Jaishankar in India to advance collaboration on roadmap priorities. This will be the 11th meeting between the two ministers since September 2025, reflecting sustained high-level engagement and a growing bilateral relationship. The visit comes as India and Canada seek to expand economic engagement and advance negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), with both sides targeting the conclusion of negotiations by the end of 2026. The two countries began the fifth round of CEPA negotiations in Ottawa earlier this month, with energy, critical minerals and aerospace cooperation emerging as key areas for expanding economic ties. Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu will also be part of the Canadian delegation, with the aim to further advance negotiations on the CEPA agreement. "This week, I’m leading Canada’s largest trade delegation to India in more than 30 years. India is home to more than 1.4 billion people and is one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies, making it a significant opportunity for Canadian businesses to reach new customers. 300 business delegates are joining me on this trade mission to India to build new partnerships in aerospace, clean energy, technology, life sciences, agri-food and forestry. We’re also advancing negotiations on a Canada-India CEPA trade agreement, with the goal of opening more opportunities for Canadian workers and businesses," Sidhu said. The negotiations follow discussions between Sidhu and Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers Meeting, where the two sides discussed the fourth round of negotiations. Canada has also set an ambitious target of more than doubling bilateral trade with India to USD 70 billion by 2030, from around USD 30 billion, as both countries seek to strengthen commercial ties and diversify economic partnerships. Last week, Sidhu said nearly 300 Canadian business delegates would join the Team Canada Trade Mission to India to explore new business opportunities and attract investment. “Nearly 300 Canadian business delegates are joining the Team Canada Trade Mission I am leading to India next week to secure new opportunities for our businesses and workers in one of the world's fastest-growing markets,” Sidhu said in a statement. The trade mission will focus on connecting Canadian expertise in key sectors with India's growing market demand, with aerospace, agri-food and clean technology identified as areas offering opportunities for greater commercial engagement and investment. “This is how we will more than double our trade with India to USD 70 billion by 2030,” Sidhu said. According to the Canadian government, two-way trade between India and Canada reached USD 30.4 billion in 2025, including USD 11 billion in goods. The two countries have shared nearly 80 years of diplomatic relations and maintain growing people-to-people ties. Against this backdrop, Anand's discussions with Jaishankar are expected to advance cooperation across the bilateral roadmap, including trade, energy, security and defence, alongside broader people-to-people engagement. During her stay in New Delhi, Anand will also participate in the Bloomberg New Economy Forum for a panel discussion on middle powers and the changing global order. She will reinforce the importance of multilateral and plurilateral cooperation amid geopolitical uncertainty and highlight Canada as a reliable partner for India and the broader Indo-Pacific. Following her India visit, Anand will travel to the UAE, where she will meet Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, along with senior leaders, government officials and business leaders. The discussions will focus on strengthening bilateral relations, expanding commercial partnerships and promoting cooperation in defence and security, artificial intelligence, innovation and people-to-people ties. (ANI)

item.title: IMF sounds alarm on mounting fiscal strains as major economies grapple with high debt
item.description: Major economies face growing pressure to rein in fiscal deficits and rebuild financial buffers as high public debt and rising borrowing costs limit their ability to respond to future shocks, the ...
item.content:encoded:
IMF sounds alarm on mounting fiscal strains as major economies grapple with high debt Major economies face growing pressure to rein in fiscal deficits and rebuild financial buffers as high public debt and rising borrowing costs limit their ability to respond to future shocks, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned, even as it projected global growth at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027. ANI | Updated: 13-10-2026 09:02 IST | Created: 13-10-2026 09:02 IST

International Monetary Fund (IMF) logo is seen outside the headquarters building in Washington, US. (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Major economies face growing pressure to rein in fiscal deficits and rebuild financial buffers as high public debt and rising borrowing costs limit their ability to respond to future shocks, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned, even as it projected global growth at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027. In its October 2026 World Economic Outlook, the IMF said public debt remained high across many economies, while fiscal deficits in several countries were significantly larger than before the COVID-19 pandemic. The report cautioned that higher financing costs were adding to concerns over the sustainability of government finances. “The global economy is again proving resilient, but unevenly so and with rapidly narrowing margins of adjustment in the near term,” the IMF said, pointing to persistent geopolitical uncertainty, higher energy prices and changes in trade policies. Global growth is projected to slow from 3.5 per cent in 2025 to 3.1 per cent in 2026 before recovering to 3.4 per cent in 2027. Global headline inflation is expected to rise to 4.7 per cent in 2026, largely due to higher energy and food prices, before easing to 4.1 per cent next year. The Fund said governments had used fiscal buffers to absorb repeated shocks, including the pandemic and subsequent disruptions. However, spending pressures linked to ageing populations, climate change and national security needs remain, leaving less room for governments to respond to fresh crises. “Fiscal policy must be restrained and help contain demand pressures at a time of heightened inflationary risks,” the report said, stressing the need for governments to strengthen their finances as borrowing costs rise. The IMF also warned that global trade growth would face pressure from tariffs and adjustments in production chains, although technology-related trade was expected to provide some support. It said global imbalances were likely to decline only modestly over the medium term, with large fiscal deficits and differences in domestic demand continuing to sustain external gaps. Risks to the outlook remain tilted towards weaker growth. A prolonged or intensified conflict in the Middle East could keep energy and food prices elevated, revive inflationary pressures and worsen fiscal balances. A sharp reassessment of returns from artificial intelligence-related investment could also reduce investment and tighten financial conditions. The IMF called for “strong and deliberate actions” to rebuild buffers and improve economies’ ability to withstand future shocks, warning that high debt and financing costs made fiscal adjustment increasingly urgent. (ANI)
